patient.name: Angela Rosario
patient.chief_complaint: Three months of rapidly progressive bilateral leg weakness, foot drop, and difficulty with arm elevation
patient.hpi: Angela Rosario is a 42-year-old nurse who presents to urgent neurology clinic with a 3-month history of rapidly progressive bilateral leg weakness. The symptoms began with right foot drop that developed over 1 week, followed by left foot weakness 3 weeks later. She now has difficulty raising her arms above shoulder height and reports bilateral grip weakness. She is considering stopping work as an ICU nurse due to difficulty carrying equipment. She reports associated diffuse myalgia, fatigue, and proximal arm aching. She was evaluated in her own ED 6 weeks ago with labs showing markedly elevated CK (4,800 U/L), and was told she may have 'some kind of muscle problem' and to follow up with neurology. She was empirically started on a 5-day prednisone taper by her primary care physician, which gave modest temporary improvement but symptoms recurred within 2 weeks. She notes her eyelids are slightly heavy, particularly at the end of long shifts, though no diplopia. She has had some difficulty swallowing solids over the past 4 weeks. She recently completed a 6-week course of atorvastatin 40 mg (started 4 months ago) before suspending it herself after reading about statin myopathy. A prior EMG ordered by her primary care was interpreted as 'neuropathic' by the technician (not a physician) and she was told to see neurology for neuropathy — but she suspects this is wrong given her muscle symptoms.
pmh: Hyperlipidemia (recently started atorvastatin — self-discontinued 3 weeks ago)
No prior muscle or nerve disease

Negative: bowel/bladder dysfunction, diplopia, rash (notably absent), Raynaud's, joint pain, fever.

medications.drug: Prednisone taper recently completed (5-day course from PCP — now off)

family_history: Mother: lupus (SLE). Father: hypertension. No muscle disease in family.

social_history.note: ICU nurse (20 years). Married. Non-smoker. Rare alcohol (1-2 glasses wine per week). No illicit drugs.

labs.interpretation: Abnormal values: CK (creatine kinase) 3,640 U/L (H), Aldolase 28.4 U/L (H), LDH 468 U/L (H), AST 88 U/L (H), ALT 34 U/L (H), ESR 64 mm/hr (H), CRP 18.4 mg/L (H), ANA 1:320 speckled titer (H), Anti-Jo-1 (anti-synthetase) POSITIVE — >240 U/mL  (H), Anti-HMGCR Negative  (H), Anti-TIF1-gamma (anti-p155/140) Negative  (H).

report.summary: REPEAT EMG WITH PHYSICIAN INTERPRETATION. MYOPATHIC PATTERN — NOT NEUROPATHIC. Prior NCS/EMG misinterpreted by non-physician technician. The small, short-duration, polyphasic MUPs in proximal muscles ARE myopathic, not neuropathic. This is INFLAMMATORY MYOPATHY (polymyositis/antisynthetase myopathy), not peripheral neuropathy.

muscles_tested.spontaneous: 2+ fibrillations, 2+ PSW, occasional complex repetitive discharges
muscles_tested.recruitment: early recruitment with markedly reduced interference pattern despite weakness — MYOPATHIC
muscles_tested.morphology: small, short-duration (<8ms), low-amplitude, polyphasic MUPs (myopathic MUPs)
mixed: some myopathic MUPs — inflammatory myopathy can affect distal muscles

muscles_tested.spontaneous: fibrillations present — paraspinal involvement is classic for PM/DM

emg.summary: MYOPATHIC EMG PATTERN confirmed. Small, short-duration polyphasic MUPs in proximal muscles (deltoid, biceps, vastus lateralis). Fibrillations indicate active muscle fiber necrosis. Paraspinal muscle involvement = polymyositis/anti-synthetase myopathy. NORMAL NCS confirms this is MYOPATHY, NOT NEUROPATHY. Prior technician misread small MUPs as 'neuropathic' — this is a well-documented error; small polyphasic MUPs look different from neuropathic giant MUPs but require expert interpretation.

report.overall_impression: INFLAMMATORY MYOPATHY — anti-synthetase syndrome. NORMAL NCS excludes peripheral neuropathy. Myopathic EMG with active denervation (fibrillations from necrosis). Consistent with anti-Jo-1 polymyositis. Ptosis and dysphagia warrant MG evaluation (ACh receptor antibody, repetitive nerve stimulation, CT chest). Urgent pulmonology referral for ILD evaluation (anti-synthetase syndrome ILD can be rapidly progressive).

report.summary: Muscle biopsy left deltoid: POLYMYOSITIS PATTERN. Endomysial CD8+ T lymphocyte infiltration invading non-necrotic muscle fibers. MHC class I upregulation on all fibers. Multifocal myofiber necrosis and regeneration (perifascicular pattern absent — not dermatomyositis). No perifascicular atrophy.
report.histology: H&E: scattered necrotic fibers with phagocytosis, regenerating fibers (blue basophilic cytoplasm). Endomysial mononuclear infiltrate. CD8+ T cells on immunohistochemistry invading non-necrotic fibers (CD8 invasion of non-necrotic fibers = pathognomonic for polymyositis). MHC-I upregulation diffuse. No perifascicular atrophy (distinguishes from dermatomyositis). No granulomas. No rimmed vacuoles (excludes IBM). No capillary dropout.
report.interpretation: POLYMYOSITIS confirmed histologically. Combined with anti-Jo-1 positivity = ANTI-SYNTHETASE SYNDROME (inflammatory myopathy + ILD ± arthritis + mechanic's hands + Raynaud's). Treatment: high-dose prednisone 1 mg/kg/day + azathioprine 2 mg/kg/day as steroid-sparing agent.

report.summary: HRCT CHEST: Bilateral lower lobe predominant reticulation with ground glass opacities (GGO). Traction bronchiectasis bilateral lower lobes. Subpleural sparing partially present. Pattern: NONSPECIFIC INTERSTITIAL PNEUMONIA (NSIP) — the most common ILD pattern in anti-synthetase syndrome. No honeycombing (not UIP pattern). No consolidation.
report.interpretation: NSIP PATTERN ILD in anti-Jo-1 anti-synthetase syndrome. ILD prevalence in anti-synthetase syndrome: 80-90%. NSIP pattern has better prognosis than UIP. Pulmonology referral urgently for pulmonary function tests. PFTs needed to quantify restriction. High-dose corticosteroids + azathioprine/mycophenolate for ILD. Rituximab for refractory cases.

Neuromuscular Junction Evaluation.test: Repetitive nerve stimulation (3 Hz, right median)

Neuromuscular Junction Evaluation.value: No thymoma identified; normal thymic involution for age 42

output.interpretation: Abnormal values: Acetylcholine receptor (AChR) antibody Negative  (H), Repetitive nerve stimulation (3 Hz, right median) Decremental response: -2% (normal <10% decrement)  (H).

report.summary: PFTs: FVC 68% predicted (reduced — restriction). FEV1/FVC ratio 0.84 (normal — no obstruction). TLC 70% predicted (reduced — restrictive pattern). DLCO 58% predicted (reduced — impaired gas exchange). Pattern: RESTRICTIVE LUNG DISEASE with impaired diffusion consistent with ILD. Moderate restriction.
report.interpretation: Moderate ILD with restriction (FVC 68%, TLC 70%) and diffusion impairment (DLCO 58%). Anti-synthetase syndrome ILD confirmed. Risk stratification: moderate severity. Treatment: high-dose prednisone + azathioprine (or mycophenolate). Serial PFTs every 3-6 months to monitor progression. Rituximab for refractory/worsening ILD.

output.interpretation: Abnormal values: Anti-HMGCR antibody Negative  (H), Anti-Jo-1 (confirmatory) POSITIVE >240 U/mL  (H).

report.summary: CT CHEST/ABDOMEN/PELVIS: HRCT chest — NSIP pattern ILD (as above), no malignancy. Abdomen/pelvis: No mass, no lymphadenopathy, no organ abnormality. IMPRESSION: No occult malignancy identified. Anti-Jo-1 anti-synthetase syndrome has lower cancer association than anti-TIF1-gamma dermatomyositis (which has >50% cancer risk). Standard cancer screening (mammogram, Pap, colonoscopy) should be current. No specific malignancy workup beyond age-appropriate screening required for anti-Jo-1.
report.clinical_significance: Anti-TIF1-gamma was negative — the high-risk paraneoplastic antibody is absent. Anti-Jo-1 has low (<15%) cancer association. Age-appropriate screening recommended.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Anti-synthetase syndrome (anti-Jo-1 polymyositis with ILD) — misattributed to peripheral neuropathy
critical_actions: Do NOT accept 'neuropathy' diagnosis when CK is 4800 U/L and weakness is proximal predominant — this is myopathy
Repeat NCS/EMG with physician interpretation — myopathic MUPs were misread as neuropathic by non-physician technician
Order anti-Jo-1 and full myositis antibody panel — this is the primary diagnostic test
Order HRCT chest urgently — ILD can be rapidly progressive in anti-synthetase syndrome and causes significant morbidity/mortality
Evaluate for MG overlap (ptosis, dysphagia) — AChR antibody and RNS
contraindicated_actions: Do not diagnose as peripheral neuropathy based on misread EMG — normal NCS excludes significant neuropathy
Do not attribute to statin myopathy without checking anti-HMGCR — statin was 4 months only; primary diagnosis is anti-synthetase syndrome
Do not miss ILD evaluation — 80-90% of anti-synthetase syndrome patients have ILD which is the leading cause of death
Do not use ice pack test result to diagnose MG without AChR/MuSK antibodies — ice pack test is non-specific and can be positive in any cause of ptosis

differential.key_distinguishing: Normal NCS; myopathic not neuropathic EMG; weakness is proximal predominant (deltoids, hip flexors) not distal; no sensory loss; CK markedly elevated (neuropathy does not elevate CK significantly)
Anti-HMGCR negative; anti-SRP negative; statin was only 4 months (short duration); biopsy shows inflammatory cells invading fibers (PM pattern) not pure necrosis (IMNM pattern)
Ptosis from levator myositis not NMJ dysfunction; AChR/MuSK antibodies negative; no decremental response on RNS; ice pack test can be false positive in non-MG ptosis

No classic skin rash (Gottron's papules, heliotrope, V-sign, shawl sign — all absent); no perifascicular atrophy on biopsy; anti-Mi-2 and anti-TIF1-gamma negative; anti-Jo-1 positive (more typical of PM/antisynthetase)

key_reasoning_points: DIAGNOSTIC PUZZLE: Three compounding misdirections — (1) non-physician EMG misread myopathic MUPs as neuropathic, (2) atorvastatin history led to statin myopathy attribution, (3) ptosis/dysphagia raised false MG concern
CRITICAL CLUE IGNORED: CK 4,800 U/L (18x ULN) — peripheral neuropathy does NOT elevate CK; only myopathy or motor neuron disease elevates CK significantly
PROXIMAL WEAKNESS DISTRIBUTION: Deltoids 3+/5, hip flexors 3+/5 with intact sensation = myopathy; typical neuropathy has distal > proximal and sensory + motor
EMG PITFALL: Myopathic MUPs (small, short, polyphasic) can be mistaken for neuropathic by inexperienced readers; expert physician interpretation is essential
ANTI-JO-1 CLINICAL SYNDROME: Not just myositis — includes ILD (90%), Raynaud's, inflammatory arthritis, mechanic's hands; must evaluate all components
ICE PACK TEST: Positive in any ptosis (cold improves acetylcholinesterase activity) — non-specific for MG; AChR antibody and RNS are the definitive tests
STATIN TRAP: 4 months of atorvastatin + elevated CK = statin myopathy assumption; anti-HMGCR must be checked; in this case, statin was coincidental (pre-existing anti-Jo-1 syndrome)
